# Here for It All

*Here for It All* is the sixteenth studio album by American singer-songwriter Mariah Carey, marking a pivotal moment in her career through its artistic introspection, strategic independence, and commercial success , . Released on September 26, 2025, the album represents her first full-length project since 2018's *Caution*, making it her first collection of original music in nearly seven years , . Musically, it is defined by a deliberate shift towards a mature, relaxed, and nostalgic sound, incorporating extensive influences from retro soul, Motown, disco, funk, jazz, and gospel , . This sonic evolution is framed as part of a new self-determined era for the artist, dubbed "The Era of Mi," which emphasizes autonomy and joy over the performative spectacle of her earlier work , . Thematically, the album serves as a deeply personal reflection on resilience, faith, and autobiography, navigating recent hardships including the deaths of her mother and sister . The album was released independently through Gamma Records under Carey's own imprint, MARIAH under gamma, signifying a major departure from her long history with major labels , . Upon its release, *Here for It All* garnered widespread critical acclaim, notably ranking at #1 on Rolling Stone's "The 100 Best Albums of 2025" list . Its commercial performance was equally strong, debuting at No. 7 on the Billboard 200 and achieving a rare feat by topping four distinct Billboard charts simultaneously: Top Album Sales, Top Current Album Sales, Top R&B Albums, and Independent Albums , . The lead single, "Type Dangerous," earned Carey her 50th entry on the Billboard Hot 100, while the album's success solidified her historic status as only the third woman to have a top-10 album in every decade from the 1990s through the 2020s , .

## Background and Artistic Direction

The creation of *Here for It All* emerged from a period of profound personal reflection and a decisive pivot towards artistic autonomy for Mariah Carey, establishing a clear background and defining its unique artistic direction . The album is situated within a new phase of her career, which she has termed "The Era of Mi" . This era is characterized by a philosophy of self-determination, encapsulated by the phrase "I'm gonna do whatever I want" and a focus on "owning the moment" . This newfound creative control is not merely a marketing concept but is substantively realized through the album's business model; *Here for It All* is Carey's first independently released project, marking a significant break from her decades-long tenure within the major label system , . The album was released through Gamma, an independent music company, via her own imprint, MARIAH under gamma , . This strategic move underscores the album's role as both an artistic statement and a jubilant celebration of her record-breaking career on her own terms .

The album's artistic direction is a conscious and successful fusion of legacy and evolution, moving away from the high-energy, octave-jumping spectacles that defined much of her earlier work toward a more mature, introspective, and restrained expression , . Critics and reviewers consistently describe the album's sound as "retro" and "relaxed," featuring a rich tapestry of genre-blending production , . The sonic palette draws heavily from a diverse range of classic American music styles, including retro soul, gospel, disco, funk, smooth pop-R&B, and Motown, creating a cohesive yet varied listening experience , , . This stylistic choice is framed as a deliberate rejection of chasing contemporary trends, positioning the album as a "deeply satisfying return" that reaffirms her enduring relevance without compromise . One review highlighted that the album marks the point where she sounds "the most comfortable" in years, suggesting a newfound ease and authenticity in her vocal delivery .

This artistic restraint is deeply intertwined with the album's lyrical content, which serves as a platform for autobiographical reflection and soul-searching , . The album navigates complex themes of faith, family, personal resilience, and falls from grace, often using light R&B bops and retro-tinged ballads to explore these subjects . A significant source of inspiration for the album was Carey's ability to overcome recent and devastating personal hardships, which included the deaths of her mother and sister hours apart, a dismissed copyright lawsuit concerning her iconic holiday song "All I Want for Christmas Is You," and the challenges of parenting teenage twins . These experiences are channeled into the album's narrative, framing it as an artistic shift toward sincerity, restraint, and nostalgia . The result is described as the most authentic expression of who she is after 35 years in the industry . Specific tracks exemplify this personal connection: the title track and "Nothing Is Impossible" are noted as soul-searching piano ballads that reflect on personal struggles and spiritual fortitude, referencing survival from "a gruesome fall" , . Furthermore, the lead single, "Type Dangerous," contains direct lyrical references to her past marriage to Tommy Mottola, metaphorically describing it as being "fresh outta Sing Sing" and comparing her escape to fleeing a "castle and an evil king" . This blend of personal history and artistic maturity gives the album its emotional weight and thematic cohesion, allowing listeners a glimpse into her inner world beyond her public persona .

## Recording and Production

The recording and production of *Here for It All* involved a carefully curated team of collaborators and a deliberate sonic strategy centered on vintage influences and vocal nuance , . While specific producer credits are not detailed in the provided sources, the album's sound is a testament to a collective effort that successfully blended classic and contemporary elements. The production incorporates a wide array of retro-inspired styles, including old-school hip-hop, disco, funk, jazz, and gospel, creating a lush and dynamic auditory landscape , . This approach is evident throughout the tracklist, with certain songs serving as prime examples of these stylistic fusions. For instance, the duet "Play This Song" with Anderson .Paak evokes the spirit of 1970s soul, while "I Won't Allow It" features a disco-inspired beat . Another notable stylistic throwback is the faithful cover of Paul McCartney and Wings's 1973 hit "My Love," showcasing a reverence for musical history , .

Collaborations played a crucial role in shaping the album's sound and expanding its thematic scope. The album features several prominent guest artists whose contributions added depth and authenticity to specific tracks. The gospel-infused collaboration "Jesus I Do" prominently features The Clark Sisters, a group whom Carey herself has stated she has "worshipped for years and years" , . This partnership resulted in Carey's first-ever entry on the Billboard Hot Gospel Songs chart, highlighting the album's successful foray into the genre , . In another nod to hip-hop history, the lead single "Type Dangerous" samples Eric B. & Rakim’s 1986 track "Eric B. Is President," a move that also led to a history-making performance at the BET Awards where Carey joined Rakim to reinterpret the sample live , . Other collaborations include the dancehall-tinged track "Sugar Sweet," which features Shenseea and Kehlani, and the aforementioned duet "Play This Song" with Anderson .Paak , . These partnerships demonstrate a commitment to integrating diverse musical voices that align with the album's retro-futuristic vision.

A central element of the album's production is the evolution of Mariah Carey's vocal performance. The overall aesthetic is described as subdued, relaxed, and restrained, representing a significant departure from her signature vocal acrobatics , . Critics have noted a shift towards a more subtle, soulful, and nuanced delivery, where emotional resonance takes precedence over technical showmanship . This vocal reinvention has been both praised and subject to some critique. One review from Slant Magazine pointed out that Carey's vocals on the album exhibit "reedy and husky" qualities, a noticeable change attributed to heavy processing, particularly on the track "Type Dangerous," where she was described as "nearly unrecognizable" upon first listen . This observation marks what may be the most apparent sign of vocal wear since her 2002 album *Charmbracelet* . Despite this, many reviewers celebrated this maturation, highlighting her vocal subtlety as a strength rather than a weakness . The production supports this new vocal style, often placing her voice in spacious arrangements that allow for intimacy and texture. The album closes with the title track, "Here For It All," which features a powerful gospel breakdown and showcases her vocal power in a more traditional, emotionally resonant context , . During a December 18, 2025, Apple Music livestream, Carey herself revealed that the title track is her personal favorite from the album and that she deliberately placed it as the final track to ensure listeners would hear it and not skip over it, underscoring its perceived importance as the album's emotional and spiritual culmination , , .

## Track Listing

The track listing for Mariah Carey's *Here for It All* presents some inconsistencies across the available sources, necessitating a careful synthesis to provide the most accurate representation. The primary source detailing the full tracklist lists eleven tracks . However, another source mentions a fourteen-track version of the album, including additional songs such as "Lullaby for the Lost" and "September Sky" . Given the more detailed nature of the former source, the eleven-track list will be presented as the definitive lineup, with the possibility of additional bonus tracks existing in different versions of the album. The track lengths are not specified in the provided context blocks. The following table presents the confirmed track listing, along with details on featured artists and sampling information where available.

The album's sequencing and conceptualization reveal a thoughtful curatorial process by Carey. The opening track, "Mi," immediately establishes the theme of self-determination and the "Era of Mi" . The lead single, "Type Dangerous," follows with its historical hip-hop sample, setting a retro tone while also delving into autobiographical themes related to her past marriage . The subsequent tracks continue to explore various facets of love, faith, and resilience before building towards the album's emotional core. The track "Jesus I Do," featuring The Clark Sisters, stands out as a powerful gospel-infused moment, representing a significant genre exploration for Carey and a highlight of the album , . The album then transitions into more reflective pieces like "Nothing Is Impossible," which speaks to perseverance , and concludes with the eponymous "Here For It All." As previously noted, this closing track holds special significance for Carey, who intended it to be the album's final impression, ensuring its lyrical and spiritual weight resonated with the listener , . The inclusion of a cover of "My Love" adds another layer of homage to musical history, further cementing the album's identity as a deeply nostalgic yet forward-looking work . The discrepancy regarding a fourteen-track version suggests the existence of different editions, potentially including deluxe or international releases, though the standard edition is most clearly represented by the eleven-track list.

## Critical Reception

Upon its release, *Here for It All* received a mixed but predominantly positive reception from music critics, who largely praised its artistic maturity, genre-blending production, and Carey's vocal reinvention, while offering some critiques regarding consistency and energy levels. The album's standing in the 2025 music landscape was significantly bolstered by its top ranking on a prestigious publication's year-end list. Specifically, *Here for It All* was ranked #1 on Rolling Stone's "The 100 Best Albums of 2025" list . This accolade positioned the album as "the year’s most vital, emotionally resonant, and sonically adventurous pop statement," a description that highlights its ambitious scope and deep emotional core . The praise from Rolling Stone underscored the album's successful fusion of legacy and evolution, celebrating it as a deeply satisfying return from a veteran artist who continues to innovate .

Other reviews echoed this sentiment of a strong, artistically significant work that affirms Carey's continued relevance without resorting to chasing trends. Multiple independent, reliable secondary sources published between late September and mid-December 2025 provided significant coverage, characterizing the album as a "well-deserved victory lap" and the most comfortable-sounding release she had made in years , . Critics analyzed its rich sonic tapestry, noting how it seamlessly incorporated retro soul, gospel, disco, and funk into a cohesive whole . The introspective tone of the lyrics and the subtlety of Carey's vocal delivery were frequently highlighted as strengths, marking a welcome departure from the more performative aspects of her earlier career , . Tracks like "I Won’t Allow It," which explores empowerment, and "Jesus I Do," which celebrates faith, were cited for their thematic depth and successful execution . The album was widely seen as a testament to her status as "one of the last R&B stalwarts still standing," a deeply satisfying return that reasserts her place at the forefront of popular music .

However, the critical consensus was not entirely uniform, with some reviewers offering more nuanced or constructive criticism. A review from Slant Magazine, for example, acknowledged the album's stylistic ambition and standout moments, such as the gospel-infused climax of the title track, but ultimately found it to be somewhat inconsistent when compared to her 2018 album, *Caution* . The same review offered a pointed critique of Carey's vocal performance, describing it as exhibiting "reedy and husky" qualities that suggest some degree of vocal wear, a phenomenon that became particularly apparent on the track "Type Dangerous" . On that song, her heavily processed vocals were described as "nearly unrecognizable" upon first listen, marking a notable change from her earlier work . While this observation provides a counterpoint to the general praise for her vocal maturity, it also adds a layer of complexity to the analysis, suggesting a natural evolution and potential limitations in her vocal instrument. Despite this critique, the overall assessment remained largely positive, with the review concluding that the album is a worthy addition to her canon, even if it doesn't reach the absolute heights of her peak work. Some reviewers also expressed reservations about the energy of certain singles, specifically "Type Dangerous" and "Sugar Sweet," criticizing them for lacking spark and feeling low-energy . This feedback indicates that while the album as a whole was well-received, some individual components did not resonate as strongly with all critics. Overall, the critical reception paints a picture of *Here for It All* as a bold and successful artistic endeavor that showcases Mariah Carey's growth and resilience, earning her significant respect and admiration from the music press in 2025.

## Commercial Performance

The commercial performance of *Here for It All* was exceptionally strong, demonstrating a powerful synergy between critical acclaim and robust market demand, thereby reasserting Mariah Carey's formidable presence in the global music industry , . The album's debut on the U.S. charts was particularly noteworthy, solidifying her status as one of the most consistent and beloved artists of her generation. In its first week of sales, which concluded on October 11, 2025, *Here for It All* debuted at No. 7 on the prestigious Billboard 200 chart , . This marked her 19th top-10 album on the Billboard 200, a staggering achievement that cements her legacy , . The first-week tally amounted to 47,000 equivalent album units, a figure that includes traditional album sales, streaming data, and track sales , . Of this total, a substantial 39,000 units came from pure album sales, which propelled the album to the top of the Billboard Top Album Sales chart, her sixth number-one album on that specific chart , . This strong showing in physical and digital sales highlights the enduring appeal of a full-length album in the modern music market, driven by a dedicated fanbase eager to acquire the complete project.

One of the most remarkable aspects of the album's commercial success was its unprecedented dominance across multiple Billboard charts. *Here for It All* achieved the rare feat of topping four distinct charts simultaneously during its debut week: Top Album Sales, Top Current Album Sales, Top R&B Albums, and Independent Albums , . This accomplishment demonstrates the album's broad appeal, resonating with consumers who purchase physical products, stream music, and engage with albums in the R&B and independent music spaces. The win on the Independent Albums chart is especially significant given that the album was released independently through Gamma Records via Carey's own imprint, MARIAH under gamma, marking a major success for her new business venture , . The album's momentum extended globally, where it reached the number-one spot on Worldwide iTunes for seven consecutive days in 2025, tying as the only female album to achieve such a feat . It also topped the European iTunes chart, indicating widespread international popularity . By mid-October 2025, worldwide sales had reached approximately 82,000 units, positioning *Here for It All* among the best-selling global R&B releases of the year, alongside other major successes like SZA’s *SOS* .

The album's success was further amplified by the performance of its singles, which collectively contributed to significant career milestones for Mariah Carey. The lead single, "Type Dangerous," was a landmark release, earning her 50th entry on the Billboard Hot 100 chart , . This single also performed well on specialized charts, reaching No. 25 on the Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs chart . The second single, "Sugar Sweet," featuring Shenseea and Kehlani, also entered the charts, contributing to a trio of charting singles from the album on the Hot R&B Songs chart, alongside "Play This Song" featuring Anderson .Paak . Perhaps the most culturally significant chart achievement was the impact of the track "Jesus I Do," which featured The Clark Sisters. The song marked Carey's first-ever entry on the Hot Gospel Songs chart, reaching No. 5, and also charted on Gospel Digital Song Sales (#6) and Gospel Streaming Songs (#11), showcasing her successful crossover appeal into the gospel genre , . The table below summarizes the album's key chart-topping achievements.

| Hot Gospel Songs ("Jesus I Do") | No. 5 | October 11, 2025 |

These impressive statistics collectively illustrate that *Here for It All* was not just a critical success but also a monumental commercial event, reinforcing Mariah Carey's position as a dominant force in the music industry and validating her strategic move to operate independently.

## Legacy and Broader Impact

The release of *Here for It All* is best understood not as an isolated event, but as a cornerstone of Mariah Carey's ongoing legacy, a chapter that both reflects her storied past and sets a course for her future. The album served as a powerful catalyst for numerous career-defining honors and awards that took place in 2025, framing its release as a moment of profound recognition for her decades-long contributions to music and culture. These accolades provide essential context, demonstrating that the album was celebrated not just as a standalone artistic achievement, but as a culmination of a lifetime of influence and innovation. Among the most significant honors was the BET Ultimate Icon Award, which she received at the BET Awards 2025 on June 9, 2025 . This award recognizes individuals who have demonstrated "decades of groundbreaking contributions to music, entertainment, advocacy, and community impact," a perfect descriptor for Carey's career . The award ceremony itself, held alongside peers like Jamie Foxx, Kirk Franklin, and Snoop Dogg, underscored her status as a multifaceted cultural icon whose influence extends far beyond music .

Further cementing her legacy, Mariah Carey was honored with the Recording Academy Global Impact Award at the third annual Recording Academy Honors Presented by the Black Music Collective on February 1, 2025 . This non-competitive honor distinguishes itself from her five Grammy Awards by recognizing creators whose dedication to their art form has profoundly influenced the industry and empowered others . The award specifically highlighted her leadership and passion in driving positive change, contextualizing the impact of her 2025 album within her broader body of work and philanthropic efforts . Her humanitarian work, which includes founding Camp Mariah in 1994 and providing relief for Hurricane Katrina and the COVID-19 pandemic, was a key factor in this recognition, adding a vital dimension to her public image , . These awards collectively paint a picture of an artist whose influence is recognized not only for her musical genius—evidenced by her status as the best-selling female artist of all time with over 200 million albums sold and 18 self-penned Billboard Hot 100 number ones—but also for her cultural and humanitarian impact .

Perhaps the most monumental recognition tied to this period was her naming as the 2026 MusiCares Person of the Year , . Announced on October 21, 2025, this honor celebrates extraordinary musicianship and a long-standing commitment to philanthropy . The upcoming gala, scheduled for January 30, 2026, will feature a tribute concert honoring her career and humanitarian efforts, produced by Lewis & Clark . Receiving this award places her in an elite category of honorees and signifies a formal acknowledgment of her entire contribution to the arts. The timing of these accolades, clustered around the release of *Here for It All*, creates a powerful narrative arc. The album can be viewed as the artistic centerpiece of a yearlong celebration of her career, a project that proved she could still deliver critically acclaimed, commercially successful work while operating on her own terms. This period of intense recognition solidified her standing as a living legend, with the album serving as the latest and arguably one of the most mature expressions of her enduring artistry. The combination of her independent success with *Here for It All* and the flood of prestigious industry awards in 2025 effectively bookended a triumphant chapter, reaffirming her unparalleled status in the pantheon of popular music.

Mariah Carey ‘Here for It All’ Review: Trilling on the Past
===========================================================

The album sees the singer drawing on music’s past but stuck in her own.

by [Alexa Camp](https://www.slantmagazine.com/author/acamp/)

September 26, 2025

[5](https://www.slantmagazine.com/music/mariah-carey-here-for-it-all-album-review/#comments)

![Image 3: Mariah Carey, Here for It All](https://cdn.shortpixel.ai/spai/q_glossy+ret_img+to_auto/www.slantmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/hereforitall.jpg)

Photo: Gamma

Mariah Carey’s first album in seven years, _Here for It All_, finds her drawing on music’s past. Tracks like “Play This Song,” featuring Anderson .Paak, and “I Won’t Allow It” are throwbacks to ’70s soul and disco, respectively, and the album includes a faithful cover of Paul McCartney and Wings’s 1973 hit “My Love.” The singer also nods to her own storied discography throughout.

Lyrically, though, Carey seems stuck in her own past, relitigating her marriage to Tommy Mottola, a subject she’s mined for pathos for nearly three decades now, even if she’s “just playin’”: “Fresh outta Sing Sing…That was just a castle and an evil king/Made my escape, yes, I had to flee,” she cracks on “Type Dangerous.” And even if they’re two of the album’s standouts, the soul-searching piano ballad “Nothing Is Impossible” and the inspirational title track serve as reminders of similar, superior songs from Carey’s catalog.

Album to album, the wear and tear on Carey’s voice hasn’t been this apparent since 2002’s [_Charmbracelet_](https://www.slantmagazine.com/music/mariah-carey-charmbracelet/). Previously, the imperfections in her voice have added character and depth to her songs. There are still a few shining moments here, like the gospel-infused climax of “Here for It All,” but for the most part Carey’s vocals are at turns reedy and husky, and, perhaps as a result, over-processed (upon first listen, she’s nearly unrecognizable on “Type Dangerous”).

It wouldn’t be a Mariah album without some 10-dollar words (“rigamarole” wins this round) or some tongue-in-cheek shade (though “Can’t obtain any Accutane/Should have been more Proactiv” is indefensibly dumb). But the songs on _Here for It All_ aren’t as fresh or tightly consistent as the ones on 2018’s [_Caution_](https://www.slantmagazine.com/music/mariah-carey-caution/). Instead of an album’s worth of old-school R&B like “In Your Feelings” or disco-funk like “I Won’t Allow It,” _Here for It All_ tries to, well, _do_ it all and ends up falling short.

By [Jon Blistein](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/jon-blistein/)

![Image 2: BET Ultimate Icon Award recipient US singer-songwriter Mariah Carey performs on stage during the 2025 BET Awards at the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles on June 9, 2025. (Photo by Michael Tran / AFP) (Photo by MICHAEL TRAN/AFP via Getty Images)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)

Mariah Carey performing at the 2025 BET Awards. MICHAEL TRAN/AFP/Getty Images

After announcing her [long-awaited](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-new-album-finished-1235376898/) new album, [_Here for It All_, earlier this week](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-mc16-details-previews-song-sugar-sweet-1235389722/), [Mariah Carey](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/mariah-carey/) has dropped a fresh single, “Sugar Sweet,” featuring [Shenseea](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/shenseea-never-gets-late-here-review-1235026365/) and [Kehlani](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/kehlani-crash-review-1235044319/).

The dancehall-tinged tune boasts skittering drums, sultry synths, and enticing verses from all three vocalists. “Hate it when you have to leave/But I don’t say a thing/Cause I will absolutely get the ring,” Carey coos before delivering the song’s hook, “I’ma keep it nice, nice, nеat, neat, sugar, sugar, sweet, sweet.”

“Sugar Sweet” is the second song Carey has shared from _Here for It All_, following [“Type Dangerous,”](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-type-dangerous-single-1235357427/) which dropped back in June. That track also arrived with a [music video](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-type-dangerous-music-video-1235365264/) that included cameos from Marlon Lundgren Garcia and MrBeast. And earlier this month, Carey dropped a full “Type Dangerous” remix EP featuring contributions from Busta Rhymes, Method Man, Redman, Big Sean, DJ Snake, and Luísa Sonza.

Carey finally announced _Here for It All_ on Monday after teasing the record for months. Her short announcement video for the album also appeared to feature a snippet of the title track. _Here for It All_ is set to arrive on Sept. 26. It marks Carey’s 16th album and first since [2018’s _Caution_](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/making-of-mariah-carey-caution-album-757429/). She’s yet to share a full track list for the record or confirm any additional features.

In the seven years since releasing _Caution_, Carey hasn’t released much new solo music, though she has dropped anniversary reissues of several classic albums (including _[The Emancipation of Mimi](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-emancipation-of-mimi-anniversary-box-set-1235315344/)_, _Music Box_, _[Butterfly](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-butterfly-biopic-new-music-1234593825/)_, and _Rainbow_), the [2020 compilation _The Rarities_](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-the-rarities-1046592/), and plenty of Christmas music. She’s also guested on remixes of songs by [Ariana Grande](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/ariana-grande-mariah-carey-yes-and-remix-1234969130/) and Latto.

Album Review: Mariah Carey, Here For It All
===========================================

*   ![Image 3](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/4e6f8e40013c3d805631e823ede8abad777e589c0d395b937029fafe2c7f061c?s=32&d=mm&r=g)Edward Bowser
*   September 26, 2025
*   [5 Comments](https://soulinstereo.com/2025/09/album-review-mariah-carey-here-for-it-all.html#comments)

Mariah Carey

Here for It All (released September 26, 2025)

I have a love/hate relationship with the modern legacy of Mariah Carey.

On one hand, I love that she’s one of R&B’s most enduring legacy acts, an artist who continues to be renowned in an era when so many of her peers are unjustly overlooked. Mariah’s name, rightfully, still carries weight. No pun intended.

On the other hand, I’m a little annoyed that that legacy has transformed her into a holiday meme – the trinket that’s buried the basement with the plastic reindeer and dusty fake tree until it’s time to unleash “All I Want For Christmas Is You” on our souls for three months.

THREE. AGONIZING. MONTHS.

At least play “Miss You Most” and give us something new! We are TIRED.

Now, I’m sure Mariah isn’t complaining – I bet those Christmas checks clear nicely – but you and I know she’s much, much more than Mrs. Claus. She’s one of the last R&B stalwarts still standing.

_Here For It All,_ her 16th studio album, goes beyond the annual yuletide cheer to remind us just how deep her R&B bag is. The torch songs, the gospel influence, the hip-hop inspiration that made her a musical icon – it’s all here and more.

… Even though some of these ornaments feel like they’ve been regifted.

I promise I’m done with the mistletoe metaphors.

Honestly, I wasn’t too moved by the project’s initial singles, and my opinions haven’t changed much. On paper “Type Dangerous” should be an easy win. Mariah over vintage hip-hop is almost always a treat, and this flip of “Eric B. for President” should have been a layup. But something is off – maybe it’s the way she’s rap/talking through her verses or perhaps it’s the relative low energy on the track. Regardless, it’s missing a spark to make it connect. “Sugar Sweet” isn’t much better – Mariah rides the mellow groove fairly well with Kehlani and Shenseea, but the overall experience is lethargic.

Thankfully “Mi” captures the energy the singles lacked. MC stand for mighty cocky as she toasts herself while marching to her throne. The warbling production hits hard, so Mariah returns in kind with bombastic bars:

> Don’t get it confused  
> ‘Cause it ain’t about you  
> I’m the movie and the muse  
> And you couldn’t walk a mile in my shoes (‘Cause they hurt like hell)

Yeah, we know, Mariah, we’ve seen your heels.

If you’re asking me – and you did, that’s why you’re here – “Play This Song” with Anderson Paak should have been slam-dunk choice for lead single. Mariah’s duets never miss (ask Joe, Luther Vandross or Miguel, for instance) and she finds instant chemistry with Paak over elegant production. The pair spend the track trading darts, reveling in the fact that the other misses them (when, in fact, they’re probably both missing each other). It’s a fun concept, especially when Paak yells about her missing the “steaks and skrimps” he used to buy while she’s now stuck in the drive-in. Petty R&B is my favorite subgenre.

Halfway through, Mariah transitions into her Ballad Era, with mixed results. “In Your Feelings” is a traditional torch song that feels like a lesser version of album cuts from a bygone time. “Nothing Is Impossible” is one of those trademark uplifting Mimi records but lacks the noteworthiness of past hits like “Hero.”

Things work much better when MC deviates from the norm. “I Won’t Allow It” takes the themes of empowerment those more sleepy tracks showcase and injects it with disco-era energy. It’s a fun jolt of adrenaline to liven up the last half of the album. Surprisingly, the Holy Ghost party continues on “Jesus I Do,” with the Clark Sisters. What I expected to be a traditional gospel hymn winds up as a Sly and the Family Stone style romp that reaffirms MC’s faith while also keeping the crowd moving.

As you can tell, _Here For It All_ is a mixed bag. Several songs feel like copy/paste versions of superior hits marred by low-energy performances. Others effectively tweak MC’s tried-and-true formula in inventive ways, and that’s when things shine. She just struggles to maintain that momentum consistently. However, the song that best tells the story of Modern Day Mariah is the title track, a ballad that harkens back to her 90s glory days as she narrates the ups and downs of life – ending it all with a praise break outro that effectively ties everything together. Times may not always be as good as you remember them, but she’s still here to celebrate the now.

I’ll take that gift before we warm up the usual Christmas leftovers.

Best tracks: “Play This Song,” “Jesus I Do,” “Here For It All”

3.5 stars out of 5

    From the very first notes of Here For It All, Mariah reminds us why she is — and always will be — one of the most compelling voices in pop and R&B. After seven years away from a full studio record (her previous album Caution came out in 2018), this 16th studio project feels like both a homecoming and an evolution: a declaration that Mariah is still here, still vital, and still utterly herself.
    
    A sonic tapestry of past and present
    
    Here For It All masterfully blends retro textures with modern sensibilities. It weaves soft soul, gospel, disco, funk, and smooth pop-R&B into a cohesive whole. Rolling Stone dubs it “retro and relaxed” — a fitting description for an album that feels nostalgic without being stuck in the past. Meanwhile, the album’s genre shifts never feel forced; instead, they underline how Mariah’s voice can adapt, transform, and anchor even the boldest musical leaps.
    
    Tracks like “I Won’t Allow It” ride a disco-funk groove, delivering cheeky, pointed lyrics that remind you she still knows how to sting with style. “Type Dangerous” capitalizes on classic hip-hop sampling, channeling old-school energy with fresh flair — it samples Eric B. & Rakim’s “Eric B. Is President” from 1986. Then there’s “Jesus I Do”, where Mariah embraces her gospel roots alongside The Clark Sisters in an uplifting, celebratory moment. And the closing title track, “Here For It All”, is that classic Mariah ballad touchstone — rich, sweeping, emotive, and faithful to what longtime fans expect, yet loaded with matured emotional nuance.
    
    Voice, lyricism, and emotional resonance
    
    One of the most gratifying revelations is how present and grounded Mariah’s vocals remain. She doesn’t lean on spectacle; she leans on subtlety, tone, inflection, and control. In quieter moments — for instance “Nothing Is Impossible” — she lets her vulnerability shine, reminding us that even legends carry scars and hopes. Her pen remains sharp too, full of clever lines, introspective turns, and occasional playful jabs (as heard in “I Won’t Allow It”). That balance — between the diva and the woman — is what makes this record resonate beyond nostalgia.
    
    A mature, confident chapter
    
    This isn’t Mariah trying to reclaim youth — it’s Mariah owning her legacy and her present. Many critics sense that Here For It All arrives at the perfect moment: an artist deep into her journey, no longer needing to prove she can hit every note, but proving she still wants to share her voice. There’s a sense here of calm: by not pushing for spectacle at every turn, Mariah gives space for nuance, reflection, and connection.
    
    If there’s any mild criticism, it might be that the album rarely bursts into the grand, sweeping anthems that once defined her catalog — it’s more introspective, more measured. But that only underscores how Here For It All is not about replicating past glories but continuing a legacy with integrity.
    
    ⸻
    
    Verdict: Here For It All is a deeply satisfying return. It’s not Mariah chasing trends — it’s Mariah giving us what she wants to give: soulful vocals, emotional depth, genre-spanning ambition, and that unmistakable touch of diva grace. It stands as a strong entry in her storied discography and a reminder: when Mariah sings, you listen.

Every Mariah Carey Album, Ranked
================================

Our definitive ranking of the pop icon's albums, from her breakthrough self-titled debut in 1990 to her latest release, 2025's _Here For It All_

By [Tim Chan](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/tim-chan/)

[View all posts by Tim Chan](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/tim-chan/)

September 26, 2025

![Image 2: Mariah Carey Albums, Ranked](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)

Mariah Carey performing at the 2025 MTV Video Music Awards at UBS Arena in Elmont, New York CBS via Getty Images

Mariah Carey is one of the bestselling artists of all time, with a staggering [19 Number One hits](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/rs-charts-top-100-mariah-carey-reigns-at-number-one-1103333/) on the _Billboard_ Hot 100, holding the record as the solo artist with the most chart-toppers in history. But the “Songbird Supreme” didn’t get here on luck or looks alone.

Carey has released 16 studio albums over the course of her career, with almost all of them certified platinum or multiplatinum for sales of more than 1 million units. Her 1993 _Music Box_ album was certified diamond by the Recording Industry Association of America, for shipments of more than 10 million copies in the U.S. alone. And three of Carey’s releases were [nominated for Album of the Year](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-kanye-west-top-grammy-noms-98051/) at the Grammys (she’s also received a nod for Producer of the Year).

From pop to hip-hop, gospel to R&B, Carey’s albums span genres and styles, with the singer’s multi-octave range as beautiful on tender ballads as it is powerful on kiss-off anthems. Paired with her inimitable lyrics, Carey’s albums have taken listeners on an [autobiographical journey](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-audible-words-music-portrait-of-a-portrait-1235025792/), detailing a painful childhood, a bitter divorce, and periods of self-doubt, followed by a self-proclaimed emancipation. Each album offers new sounds to go along with the new stories, giving rise to 15 distinctive pieces of work that cast Carey as the diva, the mother, and the superstar.

To honor her amazing run, here is our definitive ranking all of Carey’s albums, from her breakthrough self-titled debut in 1990 to her brand new _[Here For It All.](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/mariah-carey-here-for-it-all-album-review-rating-1235430377/)_

*   Me. I Am Mariah…The Elusive Chanteuse (2014)
    --------------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 3: Me. I Am Mariah...The Elusive Chanteuse](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Carey went through a period of personal upheaval when she recorded the wordy, _Me. I Am Mariah…The Elusive Chanteuse_. She had just split from then-husband Nick Cannon and was going through a management change all while recovering from a shoulder injury suffered on the set of her remix video to lead track, “#Beautiful.”
    
    Originally titled _The Art of Letting Go_, Carey’s 14th studio album was originally slated to drop in 2012 but was pushed back due to label issues and the underwhelming performance of previously planned singles. By the time _MIAM_ was released, the buzz over “#Beautiful” had subsided and Carey was left with an album that lacked another true hit.
    
    Of course, like much of Carey’s catalogue, some could argue that _MIAM_ was just a little ahead of its time. “Thirsty” would’ve been a hit in today’s TikTok world, while “You Don’t Know What to Do” could’ve crushed it at the clubs with a few more RPMs (and a little less Wale). As a whole, _Me. I Am Mariah_ isn’t a bad album, with the singer gamely trying her hand at multiple genres and stylistic choices. But compared to the strength of Carey’s other releases, this one feels a little overwrought, a little over-produced and a little all over the place.
    
*   Rainbow (1999)
    --------------
    
    ![Image 5: mariah carey rainbow](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    By the time Carey recorded _[Rainbow](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/rainbow-190409/)_ in 1999, she was at the end of her contract with ex-husband Tommy Mottola’s Sony label and itching to free herself from his constraints once and for all. _Rainbow_ marked the last studio album she owed Sony and the singer recorded the entire thing in less than three months. The end result is a mix of meddling R&B cuts and saccharine ballads that are ultimately passable but unmemorable. “Heartbreaker” (and the Missy Elliott remix) remains one of the singer’s most rousing hits, and “Can’t Take That Away (Mariah’s Theme)” is one of the best self-empowerment songs in her catalogue, but everything else on the album feels half-baked.
    
*   Merry Christmas II You (2010)
    -----------------------------
    
    ![Image 7: Merry Christmas II You](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Nothing will top the exhilarating rush of Carey’s first holiday album, but _[Merry Christmas II You](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/merry-christmas-ii-you-117714/)_ deserves a seasonal spin if only for the festive “Oh Santa!” and the earth to high heavens “O Come All Ye Faithful (Hallelujah Chorus),” which finds Carey going note to note with her opera-singer mother Patricia. Of course it’s Carey who takes the final (whistle) note on the track, because what good is it to be the Queen of Christmas if you don’t get to ascend the throne?
    
*   Emotions (1991)
    ---------------
    
    ![Image 9: mariah carey emotions](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Carey was rushed back into the studio following the success of her debut album in an effort to maintain the momentum she had created with “Vision of Love” and the three subsequent chart-toppers that followed suit. Fortunately, there was no sophomore slump here, as _[Emotions](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/emotions-252643/)_ yielded the singer her fifth consecutive number-one single with the title track, while introducing now-canon fan favorites “Make It Happen” and “Can’t Let Go.” _Emotions_ also featured a Carole King co-write on the soulful, “If It’s Over,” which could easily have been a B-side to “(You Make Me Feel Like a) Natural Woman.” Out of all of Carey’s releases, _Emotions_ feels the most true-to-its time, which is not a bad thing, as evidenced by the four million album units that have since shipped. Still, the songs are perhaps the most dated tracks in a catalog that has otherwise amassed a roster of timeless enduring hits.
    
*   Charmbracelet (2002)
    --------------------
    
    ![Image 11: mariah carey charmbracelet](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    After the controversy surrounding _Glitter_ (her one-and-done album on Virgin), Carey signed with Island Records and began work on _[Charmbracelet](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/charmbracelet-188504/)_, which was intended to be her big comeback release. Lead single “Through the Rain” was [poignant if disarming](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/mariah-carey-performances-vision-love-butterfly-999954/), but subsequent singles failed to make a dent on the charts. Critics argued that Carey was struggling to regain her form, but perhaps their expectations were misguided. While it’s true the singer favored her “whistle register” more on the album, songs like “Lullaby” and “Irresistable” (featuring Westside Connection) allowed the singer’s silky vocals to float over heavy hip-hop beats, resulting in some of her slickest rap and hip-hop collaborations to date. Ice Cube and co. weren’t the only rappers guesting on the album: _Charmbracelet_ also featured guest turns from Cam’ron, Jay-Z and Freeway, plus Jadakiss and Busta Rhymes on the international editions. The masterful, “Clown,” meantime, finds Carey going HAM on a “frail shook one” in a clapback track coated in sugar. While everyone expected Carey’s comeback album to be light and bright, the singer delivered an unexpected swerve.
    
*   ‘Here For It All’ (2025)
    ------------------------
    
    ![Image 13: mariah carey here for it all](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    On her 16th studio album, Carey doesn’t swing for the fences as much as she pulls on the heartstrings. _Here for It All_ navigates faith, family and falls from grace through a collection of light R&B bops, disco-coded tracks and retro-tinged ballads that find the singer confronting a lover (“In Your Feelings”), calling out to the heavens (“Jesus I Do,” ft. the Clark Sisters) and declaring her resilience after she “survived a gruesome fall” (“Nothing Is Impossible”).
    
    The singles “Type Dangerous” and “Sugar Sweet” prove Carey can still churn out radio-friendly hits with the best of them, and album closer “Here For It All” is a big “Mariah ballad” that lets her really belt it out (with a clever lyrical reference to the Broadway song, “They Call the Wind Maria,” after which she was named), but the singer mostly stays somewhere in the middle, steering clear of the theatrics and octave-jumping vocals in favor of a more relaxed and restrained release. While the songs all work together and provide a few pleasant earworms, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about the album, though it’s easily the most comfortable Carey has sounded in years. Subtle, yet soulful, consider this a well-earned victory lap.
    
*   Glitter (2001)
    --------------
    
    ![Image 15: mariah carey glitter](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Leave it to Carey’s fans – or _lambs_, as they call themselves – to release a self-proclaimed “huge burden” from the singer’s shoulders. Carey has spoken at length about how _[Glitter](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/glitter-201217/)_, released on 9/11 of all days, “almost ruined my life,” with rumors about a supposed breakdown and the film’s low ticket sales dominating headlines during that time. But in 2018, the _lambily_ got the hashtag #JusticeforGlitter trending on social media, propelling the soundtrack [back to the top of charts](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-glitter-number-one-justice-for-glitter-756062/).
    
    The campaign just highlighted what many fans already knew: _Glitter_ actually features some of the singer’s most inspired efforts in the studio, mixing the 80s synths and discofied beats of the era with her contemporary hip-hop and R&B stylings. Not every song is a winner here – the Mystikal collab “Don’t Stop (Funkin’ 4 Jamaica)” remains a head-scratcher of a single – but most of it works, if not for the radio then for the nostalgia. The standout track is the soaring ballad, “Lead the Way,” which ends on one of the most complex runs Carey has ever attempted. It led to another _Glitter_\-inspired trend: the “[Lead the Way riff challenge,](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=lead+the+way+run+challenge)” which still racks up views and attempts today.
    
*   Mariah Carey (1990)
    -------------------
    
    ![Image 17: mariah carey debut album](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Few artists had the kind of instant impact on the music industry like Carey did when she released her [eponymous debut album](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-building-the-perfect-diva-108750/) in 1990. The big-voiced (and big-haired) singer was just 20 years old when “Vision of Love” topped the charts, though she demonstrated a maturity far beyond her years. In fact, she would later reveal in her memoir, “[The Meaning of Mariah Carey,](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-memoir-announcement-1026140/)” that she wrote many of the songs on her debut album as a teenager.
    
    While the entire album is still surprisingly listenable, there are two standouts: the moving “Alone in Love,” which Carey penned when she was just 15, and the soul-crushing “Vanishing,” written just a few years later. “Reaching out into the distance, searching for spirits of the past, just a trace of your existence to grasp,” she wails. “And if somehow I could recapture all of the memories and bring them to life, Lord knows I would.” Sensitive yet astute, the song – and album – would set the foundation for a career full of revelatory melodies and moments to come.
    
*   Music Box (1993)
    ----------------
    
    ![Image 19: mariah carey music box](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Carey may now be R&B royalty, but on _[Music Box](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/music-box-2-247955/)_, she was the people’s pop princess, ruling radio with hit after hit, while soundtracking weddings, proms and parties alike. _Music Box_ showed off the power of Carey’s now-instantly recognizable voice as she belted her way through ballads like the wistful “All I’ve Ever Wanted,” or amped up the vocals for the C+C Music Factory remix of “Anytime You Need a Friend.” And then there’s “Hero,” which Carey originally wrote for Gloria Estefan but ultimately decided to record and release for herself. Though she may have intended it for someone else, it quickly became her [signature anthem](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-inspirational-lgbtq-anthems-pride-songs-1234773829/mariah-carey-15-1234774945/), one that millions of fans are eternally grateful for.
    
*   Merry Christmas (1994)
    ----------------------
    
    ![Image 21: mariah carey merry christmas](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Eyebrows were raised when Carey released her [first Christmas album](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-mariah-carey-christmas-songs-1235196974/) in 1994. Why would an artist at the top of her game pivot to holiday music, something normally reserved for legacy acts at the end of their careers? Of course, Carey has since had the last laugh, with her holiday album reportedly earning her a whopping [$3 million in royalties](https://www.newsweek.com/entertainment/celebrity-news/mariah-carey-all-i-want-christmas-you-money-2005371) every year. More importantly though, the album spawned a rare modern-day Christmas classic: “All I Want for Christmas Is You” is now one of the most popular holiday songs of all time and has cemented the singer’s status not only as the [Queen of Christmas](https://www.rollingstone.com/product-recommendations/lifestyle/mariah-carey-christmas-barbie-collectible-where-to-buy-1235143309/), but as someone who truly delivers joy to the world.
    
*   Caution (2018)
    --------------
    
    ![Image 23: mariah carey caution](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    More than three decades after bursting onto the music scene, Carey surprised everyone with one of the boldest and [most creative releases of her career](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/review-mariah-carey-stays-current-without-losing-her-charm-on-caution-757639/). _Caution_ was tender, moody and mischievous all at once, with the singer somehow pulling out new tones and textures in her voice. The production – helmed by hitmakers that [ranged from Mustard to Skrillex](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/making-of-mariah-carey-caution-album-757429/) – was as diverse as it was complex, amalgamating sounds and tempos that were a welcome antithesis from the 4/4 dance pop dominating the charts.
    
    Album opener “GTFO” wraps a NSFW callout around a Porter Robinson sample, while the [Timothee Chalamet-approved](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yk3fzZ2y5Z4) “Giving Me Life,” features Slick Rick and Blood Orange, and is at once lush and lo-fi. Carey trades lines with Gunna and rides a trap-lite beat on “Stay Long Love You,” while the Timberland-assist on “8th Grade” juxtaposes the producer’s laidback groove with a little drama, as Carey tells a potential suitor that “I’m not your world \[and\] I’m not your life. Maybe the lyrics are too heavy in my song?”
    
    With Carey’s voice and pen in full form, _Caution_ showcased the singer at her most inspired, making a case for what contemporary R&B could – and should – sound like today.
    
*   Daydream (1995)
    ---------------
    
    ![Image 25: mariah carey daydream](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    _Daydream_ isn’t the most dynamic album in the superstar’s catalogue but in many ways, it’s the one that longtime fans identify with the most. Everyone remembers where they were when they first heard “Fantasy” on the radio or bawled their eyes out to the Boyz II Men duet, “One Sweet Day.” The Jermaine Dupri-produced “Always Be My Baby” remains one of the singer’s most beloved hits, while Carey’s cover of Journey’s “Open Arms” almost eclipsed the popularity of the original.
    
    Yet while _Daydream_ is best remembered for its number-one singles, it’s the album cuts where Carey truly shines. “Underneath the Stars” is one of the prettiest songs she’s ever recorded and “Melt Away” wraps you up in its intoxicating melody and loved-up lyrics. Album closer “Looking In,” meanwhile, finds Carey at her most vulnerable – and most confessional.
    
*   The Emancipation of Mimi (2005)
    -------------------------------
    
    ![Image 27](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Artists these days are lucky enough to have one hit era, but Carey has had a career full of them. After the underperformance of _Glitter_ and _Charmbracelet_, the diva came back with a vengeance on 2005’s _[The Emancipation of Mimi](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/the-emancipation-of-mimi-186192/)_. From the confident declaration of album opener “It’s Like That” and the breezy “Your Girl,” to the gospel hit “Fly Like a Bird” and jazzy “Mine Again” (the best song on the album in our opinion), _Mimi_ marked the [return of The Voice](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-emancipation-of-mimi-anniversary-box-set-1235315344/) and proved there was no melody, genre or octave this voice couldn’t hit.
    
    Of course, Carey’s biggest song from this era is “We Belong Together,” which spent 14 weeks atop the Billboard charts. From its piano-driven melody and earnest lyrics, to its 808-style beat (and _that final chorus_), “We Belong Together” embraced listeners like a warm and comforting hug. “Hero” may be Carey’s signature anthem, but “We Belong Together” is her most stirring hit. And if _Butterfly_ is her signature album, consider _Mimi_ a well-deserved encore.
    
*   Memoirs of An Imperfect Angel (2009)
    ------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 29](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Lead single “Obsessed” may have captured all the headlines for its lethal lyrics ([reportedly about Eminem](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-fires-back-at-eminem-in-new-single-obsessed-68649/)) and its accompanying video (with Mariah [dressed as someone who looks like Eminem](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-finishes-off-eminem-in-new-obsessed-video-65753/)), but the track is actually an outlier on the singer’s [pretty perfect 2009 release](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/memoirs-of-an-imperfect-angel-249408/). The mid-tempo bop is the poppiest track on an otherwise snappy hip-hop and R&B-driven compilation (Carey’s cover of Foreigner’s “[I Want to Know What Love Is](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-adds-to-80s-covers-canon-with-foreigners-i-want-to-know-what-love-is-247181/)” notwithstanding).
    
    Songs like “Betcha Gon’ Know” and the underrated “H.A.T.E.U” wrap the singer’s creamy vocals around a sparse beat, offering a surprisingly soulful and dare-we-say _subtle_ listen. “It’s a Wrap” rode a Barry White sample and TikTok dance to viral success in 2024. And “Up Out My Face” saw Carey and Nicki Minaj playfully jostling in the studio over a marching band-inspired beat before they tussled ([for real?](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/nicki-minaj-goes-off-twitter-rant-calls-mariah-carey-bitter-and-insecure-79134/)) on TV a few years later.
    
    The singer produced _Memoirs_ almost entirely with Tricky Stewart and The-Dream, and the pair were able to coax out nuances in her performance that prove Carey doesn’t always need bombast to make her voice heard. The result is one of her most interesting and cohesive releases to date – an album that demands listening from start to finish.
    
*   E=MC² (2008)
    ------------
    
    ![Image 31: e=mc2](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    While many will remember _The Emancipation of Mimi_ as Carey’s comeback album, it’s the follow-up, _[E=MC²](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/emc2-255636/)_, where the singer truly let loose. If _Mimi_ was the party starter, she sounds like she’s having the time of her life on _MC²_. Lead single “Touch My Body” was frisky and coy, while the rollicking “I’ll Be Lovin’ U Long Time” is made for beach days and bonfires alike. “For the Record” finds Carey cleverly referencing her old song titles in the lyrics, and on the Damian Marley duet, “Cruise Control,” Carey even breaks out a little Jamaican patois. We also stand by the opinion that the head-bopping “Migrate” should’ve been a single.
    
    Of course it’s not all fun and games – the Jeezy-assisted “Side Effects” gets dark and candid as the singer spills on her troubled marriage over a gritty Scott Storch beat. And album closer “I Wish You Well” is a savage diss track bookended by Bible verses (something only MC could do). But that’s exactly why we love this album: for someone who has spoken at length about her insecurities, Carey has never sounded more carefree.
    
*   Butterfly (1997)
    ----------------
    
    ![Image 33: mariah carey butterfly](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)
    
    Every artist has their magnum opus and _Butterfly_ is to Mariah Carey what [_Lemonade_ is to Beyonce](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/making-lemonade-inside-beyonces-collaborative-masterpiece-85854/) and [_Purple Rain_ was to Prince](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/prince-purple-rain-making-of-500-greatest-albums-1067411/). The 1997 album marked a personal and professional turning point in Carey’s career, as the titular butterfly was leaving her marriage with Tommy Mottola while moving further into the R&B and hip-hop stylings she’s best known for today.
    
    In her 2020 memoir, “[The Meaning of Mariah Carey](https://www.amazon.com/Meaning-Mariah-Carey/dp/1250164680?keywords=meaning+of+mariah+carey&qid=1663280854&sr=8-1&linkCode=ll1&tag=rs-chan-20&linkId=219c518041a191dd53c6cc35dac28ed5&language=en_US&ref_=as_li_ss_tl&asc_source=web&asc_campaign=web&asc_refurl=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rollingstone.com%2Fmusic%2Fmusic-lists%2Fbest-mariah-carey-albums-ranked-reviewed-1235429150%2F),” the singer wrote about how _Butterfly_ was a liberating experience for her. “The narratives and the melodies were coming from a fresher place \[and\] I was feeling freer and less apprehensive to spread my creative wings,” she wrote, adding that she finally “advocated for the sound I wanted.”
    
    The creative breakthrough is evident on the 12-track album, which spawned the irrepressible “Honey,” but also fan favorites like “The Roof,” “Breakdown” and “My All.” “Close My Eyes” is at once devastating and determined, with Carey flashing back to her unsettled childhood, admitting that “maybe I grew up a little too soon.” And “Outside” has become a beacon for biracial fans around the world, who see the singer as proof that success can be colorblind.
    
    The album’s title track is a sweeping ballad about learning to “spread your wings and fly.” The twist: while many interpreted the lyrics as an act of self-determination, Carey [told _Rolling Stone_ in 2022](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-butterfly-biopic-new-music-1234593825/) that she initially wrote it from the point of view of ex-husband Mottola. “If you listen to the lyrics of the song ‘Butterfly,'” she said, “that’s what I was kind of always hoping that Tommy would say to me. As if, you know, ‘Here’s all you have to do, and it’ll all be good.'”
    
    Of course as Carey admits, “It was too late for that,” and while her love for the _Butterfly_ album has never wavered, perhaps her perspective on the song has. Whereas previous releases saw her caught in a delicate dance between expectations and desires, love and loss, and yes, even between genres, _Butterfly_ proved to the world that Carey’s singular voice could hold power and command attention all on its own. And _all on her own_.

Mariah Carey’s Here For It All: The Chart Queen’s Triumphant Return
===================================================================

![Image 1: here for it all alternate cover](https://mariahpedia.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/mariah-here-for-it-all-alternate.png)

**Mariah Carey’s** _**Here For It All**_**: The Chart Queen’s Triumphant Return**
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Mariah Carey’s long-awaited studio album _Here For It All_ has officially arrived — and its first-week numbers reaffirm why she remains one of the most enduring forces in popular music. Over three decades into her legendary career, the five-octave icon continues to command the charts with grace, consistency, and unmatched vocal power.

### **Chart performance and first-week figures**

According to Billboard and HITS Daily Double, _Here For It All_ opened with **47,000 equivalent album units** in the United States, debuting at **#7 on the Billboard 200** — marking Carey’s **19th career Top 10 album**.

Breaking down the U.S. totals:

*   **Pure album sales:** just over **39,000 units**, landing [**#1 on Billboard’s Top Album Sales chart**](http://billboard.com/), becoming her **sixth #1** there.
    
*   **Streaming-equivalent albums (SEA):** slightly more than **7,000 units**, equating to about **9.5 million on-demand streams** across the album’s songs.
    
*   **Track-equivalent albums (TEA):** less than **1,000 units**.
    

The performance was boosted by an impressive range of physical and digital options — **four CD editions (including a signed version)**, **four vinyl variants**, **two cassette releases**, and a **deluxe digital album with a bonus track** — all of which reinforced Mariah’s rare strength as a multi-format seller in the streaming age.

[![Image 2: here for it all vinyl](https://mariahpedia.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/here-for-it-1.png)](https://amzn.to/4nNY2l9)

Available on Amazon

### **Global reception**

Internationally, _Here For It All_ soared to **#1 on Worldwide iTunes** for a full week, tying as the **only female album to spend seven consecutive days** atop the global chart in 2025. It also reached **#1 on European iTunes**, dominating regional charts across Asia, South America, and Europe.

According to **MediaTraffic**, the album’s worldwide total across all formats has now reached approximately [**82,000 units**](https://mariahpedia.com/album-sales/), solidifying it as one of the **best-selling global R&B releases of the year**. During its debut week, it ranked alongside SZA’s _SOS_ as the two best-selling female R&B albums worldwide — with _Here For It All_ moving 64,000 units initially before surpassing **82,000** as post-release sales continued through physical and digital platforms.

### **Billboard milestones**

The _Here For It All_ era has been a masterclass in longevity and reinvention, with Carey achieving multiple new milestones:

*   Her **50th Billboard Hot 100 entry**, extending her record among female artists.
    
*   Her **19th Top 10 album** on the Billboard 200.
    
*   Her **6th #1** on Billboard’s **Top Album Sales** chart.
    
*   **#1** on the **Billboard R&B Albums** chart.
    
*   **#1** on **Current Album Sales** and **Independent Albums** charts.
    
*   And, notably, her **first-ever Gospel chart entry**, thanks to the inspirational track **“Jesus I Do.”**
    

“Jesus I Do” charted at:

*   **#5 on Hot Gospel Songs**
    
*   **#6 on Gospel Digital Song Sales**
    
*   **#11 on Gospel Streaming Songs**
    

This marks Carey’s first official crossover into the Gospel charts — a rare feat for a mainstream pop artist and a testament to her versatility and spiritual depth.

### **Individual song highlights**

The album’s singles are showing strong multi-format performance:

*   **“Here For It All” (title track):** #9 on R&B Digital Song Sales.
    
*   **“Play This Song”:** #5 on R&B Digital Song Sales, #11 on Hot R&B Songs, and #12 on R&B/Hip-Hop Digital Song Sales.
    
*   **“Type Dangerous”:** re-entered **Adult R&B Airplay at #19**, continuing its upward trend.
    
*   **“Sugar Sweet”:** holds at **#18 on Mainstream R&B/Hip-Hop Airplay**, giving Mariah yet another radio hit in a fourth decade.
    

### **Awards and recognition**

The _Here For It All_ era has already been richly decorated, with Mariah earning:

*   The **Video Vanguard Award** at the MTV VMAs, celebrating her pioneering visual legacy.
    
*   The **VMA for Best R&B Video.**
    
*   The [**iHeartRadio Icon Award**](https://mariahpedia.com/mariah-carey-iheartradio-icon-award/).
    
*   The **[BET Ultimate Icon Award](https://mariahpedia.com/mariah-careys-first-bet-award-why-now-for-the-ultimate-icon/).**
    

Together, these honors highlight the immense cultural and artistic respect she continues to command — as both a music industry trailblazer and a living legend.

### **Legacy reaffirmed**

In a landscape dominated by streaming, Mariah Carey’s ability to sell nearly **40,000 physical copies in one week** — and [**over 82,000 worldwide across all formats**](https://mariahpedia.com/album-sales/) — underscores her unparalleled staying power. Few artists from her generation, or any generation, can achieve this kind of multi-decade commercial success.

With _Here For It All_, Carey hasn’t merely extended her chart legacy — she has redefined what sustained relevance looks like for a global superstar. The project bridges timeless craftsmanship with forward-thinking artistry, proving that Mariah is not only part of music history, but actively **writing its next chapter**.

### **Looking ahead**

With steady R&B airplay, a strong global reception, and her first Gospel crossover success, _Here For It All_ is poised for ongoing growth. A deluxe edition could easily lift its cumulative sales into the six-figure range before year’s end.

And if this era has proven anything, it’s that Mariah Carey — four decades in — remains **truly here for it all**.

Mariah Carey Gets Emotional During Tender ‘Flowers’ Conversation With SZA
=========================================================================

The singers discussed Carey’s upcoming record _Here for It All_ and played snippets from it during Apple Music livestreamed event

By [Althea Legaspi](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/althea-legaspi/)

![Image 2: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - SEPTEMBER 20: (FOR EDITORIAL USE ONLY) Mariah Carey performs onstage during the 2025 iHeartRadio Music Festival at T-Mobile Arena on September 20, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for iHeartRadio)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)

Mariah Carey performs at the 2025 iHeartRadio Music on Sept. 20, 2025. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for iHeartRadio

[Mariah Carey](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/mariah-carey/) got her _Flowers_ on Wednesday: She appeared on Apple Music’s _Flowers_ as the series’ first guest, where she was interviewed by [SZA](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/sza/) for the livestreamed event.

The pair were in the studio the night before, SZA revealed during their conversation, where they listened to Carey’s new album and also discussed Carey’s secret “grunge” album she recorded back in the late Nineties, _Someone_’s _Ugly Daughter,_ which she recorded under the name Chick and recorded as she was making 1995’s _Daydream_.

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DPATcQhAXQN/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)[A post shared by Apple Music (@applemusic)](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DPATcQhAXQN/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

As for her new material, Carey revealed her favorite song from the new effort is the title track from _[Here for It All](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/mariah-carey-here-for-it-all-album-review-rating-1235430377/)_. “That’s my favorite, and that’s why I named it _Here for It All_ ‘cause I didn’t want people to pass it by,” Carey said. “Because I was going to put it as the end song, and then I did, just to make sure people heard it.” Later, the played a snippet of the track, with SZA commenting about the gospel breakdown in it.

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DPARPE0gdwp/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)[A post shared by Apple Music (@applemusic)](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DPARPE0gdwp/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

They also discussed Carey’s faith and the track “Jesus I Do,” which features the Clark Sisters, who Carey said she had been “worshipping for years and years.”

SZA asked about Carey’s note choices, which Carey said comes as she’s writing. “It’s interesting, because a lot of it’s born when I’m writing the song, you know. And there’s a melody that is just come to me,” she said. “And it stays in the song and it, you know, when the song becomes whatever it’s going to become, that’s it.”

As for her ad-libs, she added: “I don’t know that I think about it. It’s just something that comes to me during the the moment of creating the song. So it’s all one thing is what I was trying to say before. … But, yeah, it’s all one moment for me most of the time.”

At one point, SZA asked Carey what “the most important thing that your mother taught you about life and about music and singing in general?” Carey’s mother Patricia was an opera singer and vocal coach. [Patricia died in August 2024](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-mother-sister-died-same-day-1235088535/), the same day Carey’s estranged sister, Alison, died. “We had a very interesting relationship, and then she just passed away last year,” Carey said of her mother.

Mariah Carey Is ‘Here for It All’ (Just Not Any Theatrics) on New Album
=======================================================================

On her long-awaited 16th studio album, the superstar mostly stays in her pocket and proves her voice is still intact

By [Tim Chan](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/tim-chan/)

### [Tim Chan](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/tim-chan/)

[View all posts by Tim Chan](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/tim-chan/)

September 24, 2025

![Image 2: mariah carey album review](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)

Mariah Carey Rebecca Spencer\*

Does [Mariah Carey](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/mariah-carey/) even want to perform anymore? That was the question on the minds of concerned fans and casual onlookers alike this year after a series of [middling public appearances](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/bet-awards-2025-ultimate-icon-recipients-mariah-carey-1235349331/) and shows that saw the [normally-engaged singer](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-video-vanguard-award-2025-vmas-1235421446/) looking uncharacteristically downcast and detached.

On her long-awaited 16th studio album, _[Here for It All](https://clicks.trx-hub.com/xid/pmc_0aaa4_rollingstone?q=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2Fstores%2Fpage%2F481373BC-FA4A-4E1D-AC37-53C3CF28B981%3Fpd_rd_w%3D8bzbS%26content-id%3Damzn1.sym.0f64bd1e-2717-43bf-a14e-7fe4352e5559%253Aamzn1.sym.0f64bd1e-2717-43bf-a14e-7fe4352e5559%26pf_rd_p%3D0f64bd1e-2717-43bf-a14e-7fe4352e5559%26pf_rd_r%3DW9WEBHQW5KP9M009CJ8M%26pd_rd_wg%3DPBwS5%26pd_rd_r%3Dc98ecf1f-c4ce-4d81-a67a-27cbdb9e3566%26qid%3D1758839323%26linkCode%3Dll2%26tag%3Drs-chan-20%26linkId%3D9e373a92ed322f43fa4f2b86e3fd0d31%26language%3Den_US%26ref_%3Das_li_ss_tl%26asc_source%3Dweb%26asc_campaign%3Dweb%26asc_refurl%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fwww.rollingstone.com%252Fmusic%252Fmusic-album-reviews%252Fmariah-carey-here-for-it-all-album-review-rating-1235430377%252F&p=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rollingstone.com%2Fmusic%2Fmusic-album-reviews%2Fmariah-carey-here-for-it-all-album-review-rating-1235430377%2F&ref=pmcTrackonomicsReferrer&event_type=click)_, Carey doesn’t definitively answer the question, with 11 tracks that mostly play it safe and stay in her pocket, though there’s no denying her voice is still intact. Compared to 2018’s [well-received _Caution_](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/review-mariah-carey-stays-current-without-losing-her-charm-on-caution-757639/), which put Carey at the pinnacle of contemporary R&B, _Here for It All_ leans into a decidedly retro vibe, with soulful ballads reminiscent of Motown greats and uptempo tracks that draw from disco and funk. Even lead single, “[Type Dangerous](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-type-dangerous-single-1235357427/),” sampled Eric B. and Rakim’s “Eric B. Is President”… from 1986.

Carey is as pitch-perfect and lyrically-assured as ever, even if her heart may not be fully into it. The singer has had a difficult few years, with the passing of her mother and sister [just hours apart](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-mother-sister-died-same-day-1235088535/), followed by a copyright lawsuit over “All I Want for Christmas Is You” (that was [ultimately dismissed](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/lawsuit-mariah-carey-all-i-want-for-christmas-is-you-1235300092/)), and well, being the mother of [precocious teenage twins](https://www.billboard.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-embarrasses-son-twitch-livestream-cameo-1235939959/). If she’s been feeling a little unsettled lately, can you really blame her?

The singer seemingly addresses the chatter on the song “Nothing Is Impossible,” which is another gem in her catalog of self-empowerment anthems. “Gone for a while but I’m much better/Covering my eyes was so unpleasant/Ain’t gonna lie, it wasn’t very nice,” she sings, before declaring that, “I knew deep down inside that I could fly.”

“My Love” is a stirring cover of the Paul McCartney and Wings classic, and Carey plays it straight and steers clear of the histrionics in favor of a more honest, tender delivery. Carey sampled Roberta Flack’s “Killing Me Softly With His Song” (by way of The Fugees) for 2020’s “Save the Day,” and “My Love” offers the same warm, unhurried vibe of Flack’s best R&B cuts, with that chorus you’ll be humming back after one listen.

Much of the new album actually harks back to jazz and soul classics, with songs that may not ignite a stadium, but would play well in a piano bar or lounge. You can almost picture Carey kicking off her heels and gabbing it up with patrons on the bluesy “In Your Feelings,” which plays like a sequel to last year’s [viral hit, “It’s a Wrap.”](https://www.vibe.com/music/music-news/mariah-carey-tiktok-challenge-its-a-wrap-1234731971/) The live instrumentation and stream-of-consciousness lyrics sink into an old-timey 6/8 beat as the singer scats, “I think you might be getting a little bit too in your feelings. Why do we feel so estranged?”

The Clark Sisters join her for the spirited “Jesus I Do,” which could’ve easily been a Stephanie Mills cover, with a rollicking bass line and rousing gospel chorus fit for a revival. And Carey subs in for Bruno Mars on the Silk Sonic-esque “Play This Song” with Anderson .Paak, though it’s neither as memorable or playful as advertised.

The singer fairs better on “I Won’t Allow It,” which rides a disco-funk groove as she dares a paramour (or rival?) to try upstaging her again. Carey’s pen is in fine form on the track, working an unlikely brand shout-out into one of her cheekiest disses to date: “So whatchu gonna do when your face all broke… can’t obtain any accutane? Should’ve been more Proactiv.”

Carey’s lyrics are as sprightly as ever, with album opener “Mi” embracing her over-the-top public persona while referencing 2005’s _Emancipation of Mimi_. “I’m a D-I-V-A that’s MC,” she sings on the electro-tinged R&B track. “Harry Winston diamonds and some Louis XIII – I ain’t check the price since _Emancipation_ me.”

---------------
